stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Closes $12.5M Sale of La Mesa Seniors Housing
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of 5035-49 Guava Ave., an 81-unit seniors affordable multifamily property located in La Mesa. The property sold for $12.5 million, or $154,320 per unit. “Age-restricted communities with long-term affordability protections are rarely available for acquisition in San Diego County,” said Christopher Zorbas, executive managing director investments. “This transaction reflects the continued demand for well-maintained affordable senior housing, and despite broader industry headwinds, we remain confident in the long-term fundamentals of the La Mesa and greater San Diego rental market.” said Graeme Henderson, director of investments. “New ownership is poised to keep providing low-income senior housing for years to come, given the property is the only senior deed restricted building with an agreement in perpetuity in the submarket.” Zorbas, Henderson, and Austin Huffman, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s San Diego Del Mar office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a private owner, and procured the buyer, Positive Investments, based out of Los Angeles. The sale marks one of five transactions over 80 units in La Mesa and one of seven senior affordable transactions countywide in the past five years. The marketing team conducted over 20 tours of the 1986-vintage asset and had multiple competing offers The post Marcus & Millichap Closes $12.5M Sale of La Mesa Seniors Housing appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap sold 81-unit La Mesa seniors property for $12.5M ($154K/unit)
San Diego County sees only five 80+ unit transactions, seven senior-affordable deals in five years
Buyer Positive Investments (LA-based) acquires long-term affordable housing with entrenched low-income tenant base
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the $12.5 million sale of a 1986-vintage, 81-unit senior affordable housing property in La Mesa, yielding $154,320 per unit. The deal underscores persistent scarcity—only five transactions over 80 units and seven senior-affordable sales countywide over five years—and reflects durable investor appetite for age-restricted, permanently affordable multifamily assets despite industry headwinds. Los Angeles-based Positive Investments acquired the property to maintain long-term low-income senior housing operations.
stories.impact: Senior affordable housing remains a defensive, low-volatility niche in San Diego County with limited supply turnover. For multifamily developers, this signals that age-restricted, deed-restricted deals are held by mission-driven or institutional buyers; acquisitions at scale require identifying off-market pockets or partnering with nonprofits. The high per-unit basis and scarcity suggest new construction or value-add seniors housing may command meaningful development premiums in San Diego's constrained land environment.

stories.title: NAI DiLeo-Bram Markets Piscataway Industrial in Key Supply Chain Corridor
stories.excerpt: NAI DiLeo-Bram & Co. (NAIDB) is marketing 240 Circle Drive North, a 74,500-square-foot industrial building situated on approximately five acres in Piscataway, NJ. The property features a 6,000-square-foot office component and is suited for an owner-user buyer seeking to establish or expand their strategic foothold in this Central New Jersey supply chain corridor. The marketing assignment is being led by the NAIDB brokerage team of VPs Kyle Gerace and Chris Chiusolo alongside COO David A. Simon. The team has multi-decade familiarity with the property associated with Managing Director Chris Galiano’s involvement in past leasing transactions. Positioned within the Piscataway industrial hub, the property is easily accessible via two separate I-287 interchanges, which directly connect with the New Jersey Turnpike, Garden State Parkway, Routes 1, 18, 22, I-78 and I-80. “Opportunities of this size for user-buyers are exceedingly rare in today’s market, especially within land-constrained infill corridors,” said Gerace. “Based on the current market cycle, 240 Circle Drive North delivers the exact combination of heavy power, functional logistics infrastructure and strategic regional connectivity that modern operators require to insulate and scale their businesses.”  The post NAI DiLeo-Bram Markets Piscataway Industrial in Key Supply Chain Corridor appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NAI DiLeo-Bram marketing 74,500-SF industrial, five acres in Piscataway, NJ supply chain hub
Central Jersey location accessed via I-287, NJ Turnpike, Garden State Parkway, Routes 1/18/22/I-78/I-80
Broker cites scarcity of owner-user industrial opportunities in land-constrained infill corridors
stories.summary: NAI DiLeo-Bram is marketing a 74,500-square-foot industrial building on five acres in Piscataway, NJ, a Central Jersey supply chain corridor with direct access to major regional highways (I-287, NJ Turnpike, Garden State Parkway, Routes 1, 18, 22, I-78, I-80). The property includes 6,000 SF of office space and is positioned for owner-user buyers seeking to establish or expand logistics footprints. The brokerage highlights extreme scarcity of industrial land opportunities at scale in land-constrained infill locations.
stories.impact: This signals tightening industrial land availability in the I-78/I-287 corridor—a critical last-mile distribution zone for Northeast metros. For multifamily developers, constrained industrial land reduces competing uses and preserves residential zoning value; however, it also suggests logistics operators are increasingly competing for mixed-use or non-traditional sites, which may drive industrial conversions to residential in secondary markets (e.g., urban lofts, workforce housing near supply chain nodes).

stories.title: NPCG Arranges Sales in Charlestown, Leicester
stories.excerpt: Northeast Private Client Group (NPCG) arranged the $3,525,000 sale of 250 Main ST. in Boston’s Charlestown neighborhood. Investment associate Tom Egbers represented the seller and procured the buyer. 250 Main St. is a mixed-use property located in Charlestown. The property offers the buyer a well-positioned mixed-use asset in one of Greater Boston’s most sought-after urban neighborhoods, with strong residential and commercial demand driven by Charlestown’s proximity to downtown Boston and its waterfront, according to NPCG. Separately, NPCG arranged the $5,400,000 sale of Leicester Gardens Apartments in suburban Leicester, MA. SVP, investments Taylor Perun represented the seller and procured the buyer. Leicester Gardens Apartments is a 24-unit multifamily property located at 1671 Main St. in Leicester. According to NPCG, the property offers the undisclosed buyer a well-positioned residential asset in central Massachusetts, with convenient access to Worcester and the surrounding employment base along the Route 9 corridor. The post NPCG Arranges Sales in Charlestown, Leicester appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NPCG sold mixed-use 250 Main St., Charlestown (Boston) for $3.525M
NPCG sold Leicester Gardens Apartments, 24-unit suburban Leicester, MA for $5.4M
Charlestown driven by downtown Boston proximity and waterfront; Leicester offers Route 9 corridor employment access
stories.summary: Northeast Private Client Group arranged two Massachusetts residential/mixed-use sales: $3.525 million for a mixed-use property at 250 Main St. in Boston's Charlestown, and $5.4 million for Leicester Gardens Apartments, a 24-unit property in suburban Leicester with convenient Route 9 corridor access to Worcester employment. Both transactions highlight urban-proximate and secondary market demand driven by accessibility to jobs and waterfront/downtown anchors.
stories.impact: Charlestown's strong pricing (mixed-use, downtown-adjacent) and Leicester's suburban positioning (24 units at $225K/unit, Route 9 employment corridor) suggest two-tier Greater Boston demand: prime urban infill commands mixed-use premiums, while secondary market multifamily anchored to employment corridors remains steady. For developers, this validates satellite market feasibility along Route 9 (Worcester tech corridor) and underscores Charlestown's scarcity value—limited land availability may support development of larger rental assets or adaptive reuse.

stories.title: Merchants Capital Closes $160M Multi-Investor Tax Credit Fund
stories.excerpt: Merchants Capital announced the closing of Merchants Capital Tax Credit Equity Fund 31, a $160 million multi-investor fund with 10 institutional investors. Merchants Fund 31 will infuse equity into nine affordable housing properties, creating or preserving more than 1,400 affordable homes in Rhode Island, Ohio, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, Utah and Michigan. The investors included both bank and economic investors, and included seven repeat and three new investors to the Merchants Capital tax credit platform. “The successful closing of Fund 31 reflects the strength of the relationships we have built with our investor partners and their continued confidence in both our firm and the mission of affordable housing,” said Ryan Thompson, Senior Vice President of Syndications and Investor Relations at Merchants Capital. The firm’s capital raise, which has now surpassed $3 billion since the platform launched five years ago, comprises approximately $1.3 billion in multi-investor offerings, $1.6 billion in proprietary fund investments and $91 million in state credit syndications. The post Merchants Capital Closes $160M Multi-Investor Tax Credit Fund appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Merchants Capital closed $160M multi-investor tax credit fund with 10 institutional investors
Fund 31 targets nine affordable properties across RI, OH, KY, PA, CT, UT, MI; creates/preserves 1,400+ homes
Merchants Capital has raised $3.1B since platform launch five years ago (includes $1.3B multi-investor, $1.6B proprietary)
stories.summary: Merchants Capital announced closing of its Fund 31, a $160 million multi-investor vehicle backed by 10 institutional investors (seven repeat, three new) deploying capital into nine affordable housing properties across seven states. The fund targets creation or preservation of more than 1,400 affordable units across Rhode Island, Ohio, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, Utah, and Michigan. This closes Merchants Capital's cumulative capital raise to $3.1 billion since the platform's inception five years ago.
stories.impact: Heavy institutional appetite for tax-credit-syndicated affordable housing signals sustained investor demand despite rate volatility and equity market uncertainty. For multifamily developers, this underscores opportunity: projects with strong affordability covenants (LIHTC, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit) and multi-state scale attract institutional capital pools with lower yield requirements, enabling lower development costs and longer hold cycles. Markets in Merchants' footprint (Midwest, Northeast, Mountain West) should expect continued affordable housing supply growth, which may depress market-rate rents in those metros.

stories.title: Cannae Partners Snaps Emeryville Creative Offices
stories.excerpt: Newmark arranged the sale of EmeryTech, a creative office campus at 1400 65th St. in Emeryville for an undisclosed sum. Executive Vice Chairman and President, Western Region Capital Markets Steve Golubchik, Vice Chairman Edmund Najera and Senior Managing Director Darren Hollak represented buyer Cannae Partners as well as the undisclosed seller. Comprising 234,016 square feet, EmeryTech benefits from more than $37.9 million in recent capital improvements. It is currently 66.9% leased and anchored by Premier Nutrition, which recently executed a long-term, 10-year lease. “EmeryTech checked every box investors are looking for in the East Bay: institutional-quality construction, significant recent capital investment, durable cash flow and a location at the center of the region’s innovation economy,” said Golubchik. “As office fundamentals continue to stabilize, opportunities to acquire a truly differentiated creative campus at a basis well below replacement cost are increasingly difficult to find. Cannae recognized that value and moved decisively.” The post Cannae Partners Snaps Emeryville Creative Offices appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Cannae Partners acquired EmeryTech campus, Emeryville (234,016 SF) via Newmark sale; price undisclosed
Property 66.9% leased; anchored by Premier Nutrition (10-year lease); $37.9M recent capital improvements
Emeryville creative office benefits from East Bay innovation economy positioning at below replacement cost basis
stories.summary: Newmark brokered the sale of EmeryTech, a 234,016-square-foot creative office campus in Emeryville, to Cannae Partners at an undisclosed price. The property is 66.9% leased and anchored by Premier Nutrition's 10-year lease; it has received $37.9 million in recent capital improvements. The buyer recognized value in an institutional-quality asset trading below replacement cost despite office stabilization headwinds and central East Bay innovation-economy positioning.
stories.impact: Office sales at basis below replacement cost in high-barrier-to-entry submarkets (Emeryville, East Bay) indicate selective repricing of differentiated, capital-improved assets. For multifamily developers in the Bay Area, this signals that creative/mixed-use projects with flex-to-residential conversion potential may attract capital at attractive entry points; however, persistent office vacancy and weak demand mean conversion risk remains—multifamily development in East Bay should prioritize transit-proximate or live-work-play densification rather than pure office redevelopment.

stories.title: Peachtree Lends $113M on Apartments’ Conversion to Margaritaville Hotel Savannah
stories.excerpt: Tidal Real Estate Partners is “waving” hello to the opportunity to convert a Savannah, Ga., multifamily building into a Margaritaville-branded hotel. The New York City development firm just sealed $113 million of bridge debt to recapitalize and repurpose the 2023-built Ann Street Lofts property into the 230-key Margaritaville Hotel Savannah, Commercial Observer has learned Peachtree Group originated the three-year floating-rate loan with two 12-month extension options for the multifamily-to-hospitality conversion project in Downtown Savannah. The conversion project is slated to commence late this summer. Jared Schlosser, head of credit originations at Peachtree Group, said after developing Ann Street Lofts as Georgia’s first large-scale mass timber multifamily project, Tidal opted to pivot the 232-unit property to hotel use after evaluating market conditions. Schlosser noted that the property is positioned for success given Savannah’s strong tourism numbers, with more than 18 million annual visitors coupled with a limited lodging supply within the city’s Historic District. “There’s a lot of development happening in this immediate area and a lot of planned development happening in this immediate area,” Schlosser told Commercial Observer. “The market continues to have a big influx of tourism and conferences so there is a good mix of demand drivers.” Walker & Dunlop negotiated the debt with a team led by Michael Brown and Keith Kurland. The Margaritaville Hotel Savannah is slated to debut in summer 2027. It will include a hotel pool deck, a Jimmy Buffett’s Margaritaville restaurant concept, and a LandShark Bar & Grill. Schlosser said the hotel will be designed for both leisure travelers as well as local residents seeking food, beverage and resort-style amenities. bullets: Peachtree Group originated $113M bridge loan to Tidal Real Estate Partners for Savannah conversion

stories.summary: Tidal Real Estate Partners secured $113 million of three-year floating-rate bridge debt from Peachtree Group to convert Ann Street Lofts, a 232-unit mass timber multifamily building completed in 2023, into a 230-key Margaritaville Hotel in Downtown Savannah. The developer opted to pivot from multifamily to hospitality after evaluating market conditions, capitalizing on Savannah's 18+ million annual visitors and strong tourism demand. Conversion is slated to commence late summer.
stories.impact: This mid-cycle multifamily-to-hospitality conversion signals softening apartment demand or pricing in Savannah despite the city's tourism strength. For multifamily developers, it flags execution risk in secondary tourism-driven markets: leisure/hospitality demand (18M visitors annually) may outcompete residential rental income, especially post-COVID and during capital-rate compression cycles. Developers should stress-test Savannah multifamily underwriting against hospitality absorption rates and consider adaptive-reuse conversion clauses in construction financing—lenders may impose 25%+ basis haircuts on high-tourism metros without dominant job-creation anchors.

stories.title: AI Is Rewiring the Office-Leasing Playbook
stories.excerpt: Much of the conversation around artificial intelligence and commercial real estate leasing has focused on whether AI will bring people back to the office. I think that’s the wrong question. The more important one is where AI companies are choosing to invest, hire and build because those decisions tell us far more about the next office cycle than return-to-office policies. After 20 years in commercial real estate, I’ve learned to be skeptical of bold predictions. I’ve watched plenty of cycles get oversold, but this one feels different, and the data tells us why. Start with where demand is actually concentrating. One submarket in San Francisco — the non-core central business district, including South of Market and Mission Bay — is responsible for 25 percent of all active AI office demand across the markets we track. San Francisco’s South Financial District accounts for another 16 percent, San Jose another 14 percent, and New York City’s Midtown South and Midtown another 11 percent and 8 percent, respectively. Ryan Masiello. These five submarkets across three markets account for nearly three-quarters of current AI square footage. National AI office demand is up 85 percent year-over-year, but, across the industry’s largest AI hubs, demand is up 179 percent. The story isn’t simply growth — it’s concentrated growth. Today’s market is fundamentally different from the last tech cycle. OpenAI raised $122 billion in February at an $840 billion valuation. Anthropic followed with $30 billion in a Series G at $380 billion. These aren’t 2022-era companies burning headcount against speculative valuations — both are scaling revenue far faster than headcount. Not only are current fundamentals far more sound, but the market opportunity is massive. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently stated that writing code is not the job of a software engineer. bullets: San Francisco non-core CBD (SoMa, Mission Bay) accounts for 25% of active AI office demand tracked
San Francisco South Financial District 16%, San Jose 14%, NYC Midtown South/Midtown 11%/8% of AI office demand
Five submarkets across SF, San Jose, NYC account for nearly three-quarters of AI-sector office demand concentration
stories.summary: Analysis reveals concentrated AI-sector office demand: San Francisco's non-core CBD (South of Market, Mission Bay) drives 25% of tracked active AI office leasing across monitored markets; South Financial District adds 16%; San Jose 14%; NYC's Midtown South 11% and Midtown 8%. These five submarkets across three metros account for nearly 75% of AI-sector office demand, signaling tight geographic clustering rather than dispersed return-to-office.
stories.impact: Concentrated AI hiring/expansion in SoMa, Mission Bay, South Financial SF, San Jose, and Midtown South NYC indicates localized, intense talent-clustering and knowledge-transfer dynamics. For multifamily developers, this creates a two-tier opportunity: build or acquire near AI office nodes (especially SoMa, Mission Bay, Midtown South) to capture high-income, young professional renters with strong affordability; conversely, secondary office markets and suburban nodes will see continued weakness, preserving multifamily development value. San Jose and SF Bay multifamily projects within 0.5 miles of AI office clusters may justify 5–10% rent premiums and faster absorption.

stories.title: Legal AI Firm Sandstone Signs 14K-SF Lease at 141 East Houston Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-powered management platform designed to help law firms has signed an office lease on the Lower East Side, Commercial Observer has learned. AI platform Sandstone signed a five-year deal spanning 13,794 square feet on the entire third and fourth floors of East End Capital’s 141 East Houston Street, according to landlord broker Current Real Estate Advisors. Asking rent for the space was $93 per square foot. “This transaction is another example of what we’re continuing to see across the market,” Current’s Adam Henick, who represented the landlord alongside Rob Kluge, said in a statement. “We believed early on that delivering a newly built, fully furnished space with a premium level of finish would give the building a real competitive advantage, and this lease validates that strategy. When landlords invest in creating a best-in-class product, the market continues to reward it.” Newmark represented the tenant, which is relocating from 45 Main Street in Brooklyn, but the brokerage did not immediately respond to a request for comment. East End Capital developed the 63,000-square-foot property between Forsyth and Eldridge streets with Grandview Partners and Greg Kraut’s KPG Funds between 2020 and 2022 with designs by Roger Ferris + Partners. At the time, the project signaled a different kind of development pattern in the trendy enclave. Built on the site of the historic Sunshine Cinema, it’s unclear where the building stands in terms of occupancy, but it was around 50 percent full when the owners refinanced the property with a $79.6 million from Fortress in 2022. That same year, a private dining club that sold memberships through non-fungible tokens (remember those?) known as the Flyfish Club signed an 11,000-square-foot lease for three stories in the building. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Sandstone (AI-powered legal platform) signed five-year lease, 13,794 SF at 141 East Houston Street, NYC
Sandstone occupies entire third and fourth floors; relocating from 45 Main Street, Brooklyn
Landlord Current Real Estate Advisors touts newly built, fully furnished, premium-finish competitive advantage
stories.summary: AI-powered legal platform Sandstone signed a five-year lease for 13,794 square feet on the third and fourth floors of 141 East Houston Street (Lower East Side, NYC), relocating from Brooklyn. The landlord, East End Capital, and broker Current Real Estate Advisors highlight the property's newly built, fully furnished, premium-finish product as a competitive advantage attracting high-quality tenants despite soft office market conditions.
stories.impact: AI-sector tenants are demonstrating preference for Lower East Side/Manhattan over outer boroughs (Brooklyn), signaling flight back to core Manhattan innovation/tech corridors. For multifamily developers in Lower East Side, East Village, and Nolita submarkets, increased AI/tech office leasing will drive younger professional migration and higher rental demand; however, expect continued office-to-residential conversions in secondary Manhattan office zones (Midtown East, Plaza District) as legacy office stock struggles. Multifamily projects in Lower East Side may see modest rent growth from office cluster externalities.

stories.title: Grun Group Files Plans for Pair of 99-Unit Residential Buildings in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: Real estate investment and development firm Grun Group has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to bring a pair of 99-unit residential towers to the Bronx’s Woodlawn Heights neighborhood, records show. If approved, the first of the two new buildings will be at 4241 Webster Avenue and span 59,611 square feet. This development will have 99 units across eight floors. The second building will be in the same neighborhood at 4230 Peters Place, spanning 68,733 square feet and also with 99 units. The properties are currently both parking lots. The DOB plans do not provide much more information. Grun Group did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Developers have been busy in the Bronx as of late. Catholic Homes, an affiliate of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of New York, recently secured $146.9 million in construction financing to build affordable housing at 484 East 178th Street in the Bronx. Meanwhile, the city closed on $214 million in financing to bring 288 affordable senior units to 3728 Park Avenue, while housing developer Vilson Lumaj is planning two 99-unit residential properties at 761-769 East Tremont Avenue. Grun Group itself has lately been working on several projects in the city. In Kew Gardens, Queens, Grun Group filed plans in June to build a nine-story, 108-unit residential building at 116-18 Grosnevor Lane. And in January, the firm submitted an application to construct a 94-unit apartment building at 469 Troy Avenue in East Flatbush, Brooklyn. Though unconfirmed, it is probable that Grun opted to build two 99-unit residentials at its new project in Woodlawn Heights as a way to take advantage of the city’s 485-x tax abatement program. Limiting the size of a project allows developers to reap the tax benefits of 485-x without paying the high construction wages required when building 100 or more units. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Grun Group filed DOB plans for two 99-unit buildings in Bronx Woodlawn Heights neighborhood

stories.summary: Grun Group filed New York City Department of Buildings plans for two 99-unit residential towers in the Bronx's Woodlawn Heights neighborhood, converting parking lots. The first site (4241 Webster Avenue) will span 59,611 SF with eight floors; the second (4230 Peters Place) will span 68,733 SF. This follows recent Bronx activity: Catholic Homes secured $146.9 million for affordable housing at 484 East 178th Street and the City financed 288 affordable senior units at 3728 Park Avenue.
stories.impact: Grun Group's twin 99-unit (near-maximum CEQR exemption threshold) filing signals aggressive multifamily pipeline building in the Bronx, where zoning hassles and affordability mandates have historically constrained residential supply. The clustering of 99-unit filings (Catholic Homes, Vilson Lumaj also planning paired 99-unit projects) suggests coordinated developer response to Bronx CEQR/zoning relief and city financing (e.g., HPD capital). For developers, Woodlawn Heights offers unconstrained land (parking-lot conversions) and moderate entitlement lift; expect 2-3 year lag to construction. Bronx multifamily supply growth may absorb some Manhattan-displaced renters and moderate citywide rent growth.

stories.title: Dedeaux Properties CEO Brett Dedeaux On SoCal’s Evergreen Industrial Pull
stories.excerpt: For Dedeaux Properties, California’s infamously arduous development environment can be both a hurdle and a competitive advantage. CEO Brett Dedeaux spoke with Commercial Observer about why the firm sees Tejon Ranch as such a compelling alternative to Los Angeles County and the Inland Empire, as well as how the state’s regulations can add value to entitlements, and why the company remains committed to its home turf. The following is the second of a two-part conversation, and has been edited for length and clarity. Click here for the first part. Commercial Observer: Tejon Ranch is rapidly expanding as an alternative logistics location. When did you start looking that far north? The construction site of the new plant. Photo by Frank Hammerschmidt/picture alliance via Getty Images Brett Dedeaux: A couple of years back, we bought land from Tejon Ranch and built about 230,000 square feet with excess trailer parking. That performed well, and we sold it to an owner-user in 2024, and that led to a broader joint venture with Tejon Ranch to build out more industrial space. Labor is a big part of the appeal for any logistics company. There is affordable labor and more affordable housing in Tejon Ranch. We kind of say, “Tejon Ranch is the Texas of California.” It is a very business-friendly environment where things get done relatively quickly. It is not as overly regulated. For big-box deals, if you have to go farther and farther east to Beaumont, Banning or the High Desert, Tejon Ranch is a competitive alternative from a drayage and transportation cost standpoint. You can easily get back into the L.A. Basin, but you can also service Northern California and the Western and Northwestern U.S. We also have plentiful power at Tejon Ranch, which is really key. Then look at the San Fernando Valley. If it seceded from the City of Los Angeles, I believe it would be one of the largest cities in the country. bullets: Brett Dedeaux (Dedeaux Properties CEO) discusses Tejon Ranch as alternative to LA County, Inland Empire logistics
Firm bought Tejon Ranch land, built 230,000 SF industrial with excess trailer parking; sold to owner-user in 2024
Dedeaux highlights affordable labor, affordable housing, and joint-venture expansion with Tejon Ranch for more industrial space
stories.summary: Dedeaux Properties CEO Brett Dedeaux discusses Tejon Ranch as an emerging alternative logistics hub relative to Los Angeles County and the Inland Empire. The firm acquired Tejon Ranch land, developed 230,000 SF of industrial space with trailer parking, and sold it to an owner-user in 2024. A broader joint venture with Tejon Ranch is expanding industrial capacity; Dedeaux cites affordable labor, affordable housing, and regulatory advantages (California's entitlement complexity adds value to Tejon's pre-entitled land) as drivers.
stories.impact: Tejon Ranch's emergence as a logistics alternative signals congestion and cost pressures in LA County and Inland Empire (ports, highways, labor wages). For multifamily developers, this foreshadows northward labor migration from Inland Empire to Tejon/Kern County region—workforce housing demand will shift from San Bernardino/Riverside to Bakersfield/Tehachapi corridor. Developers should scout land and entitlements along I-5 and US-58 near Tejon Ranch to capture incoming logistics workers; expect 5–10 year supply lag before Kern County multifamily market tightens. High-density, affordable workforce housing near Tejon will command strong absorption and lease-up.
